prime.problem: ZeRO fits the state, but a 405B run needs thousands of GPUs for FLOPs, sequences long enough that activations overflow any one GPU, and a global batch too small to hide DP traffic at 16K GPUs. No single split survives all of that; each axis runs out of bandwidth or memory somewhere.
prime.fits: Builds on ZeRO/FSDP (the DP axis) and course 6's Megatron cards (TP for serving). This card asks what changes when every split also has to carry a backward pass, keep activations, and flush at every optimizer step.
expect: TP + sequence parallelism inside a node
prime.goal: Pick a degree for each axis from a symptom (doesn't fit, too long, comm stops hiding), place each on the network tier that fits its traffic, and compute a pipeline's bubble.

attend: What does training add that makes pipeline bubbles matter, when course 6 said serving pipelines never drain?
Why does 1F1B change the memory held at GPU 0 but not the step time?
SP saves activation memory at no extra bandwidth. Which identity makes that true?
With a causal mask, why does a sequential CP split leave one GPU with 7× the work of another, and how does zig-zag fix it?
Llama 3 used 16,384 GPUs for a model whose state is only 7 GB per GPU. What were the GPUs for?

must: A training step must finish every micro-batch's backward before the optimizer steps → the pipeline fills and drains every step → idle time (p−1)/m of the useful time (37.5% for p = 4, m = 8) → more micro-batches or v interleaved chunks per GPU shrink it, at the cost of memory or v× more sends

TP splits each matmul → its collectives sit inside every layer, forward and backward, on the critical path → it only works on NVLink (≤ 8-way; ~43% drop cross-node) → TP innermost, PP and FSDP across nodes, DP outermost

Activations grow with s → at 128K even TP+SP with recompute overflows → CP splits the sequence for the whole model, and only attention needs other GPUs' K/V → causal masks unbalance a sequential split → zig-zag pairs an early chunk with a late one (1.75 → 1.00 slowest/mean)

Fixed global batch (16.8M tokens) spread over more GPUs → fewer micro-batches per pipeline or fewer tokens per DP rank → bigger bubble and less comm hiding → MFU falls (Llama 3: 43% at 8K GPUs → 41% at 16K → 38% with CP16)
elevated: 1F1B starts each backward as early as possible → GPU 0 holds p micro-batches instead of m (4 vs 8) → same 33-unit step, but the memory saved is spent on more micro-batches, which is what actually shrinks the bubble
PP moves one activation per stage boundary while ZeRO-3 re-gathers weights per micro-batch → the two combine badly → pipelines pair with ZeRO-1 (DeepSeek-V3: PP16 × EP64 × ZeRO-1, no TP)
reference: the zero-bubble and DualPipe bubble formulas
the C/W values 2,200 / 2,475 / 2,550 and the resulting TP limits

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the layout box for Llama 3 405B: which axis is innermost and which outermost, what each one sends, and over which link. Then write the bubble formula and one sentence on why it only matters in training.
checklist: TP 8 inside a node on NVLink (collectives every layer); CP and PP across nodes; DP/FSDP outermost
PP sends one activation (and one gradient back) per stage boundary per micro-batch
bubble = (p−1)/(v·m); 1F1B keeps p micro-batches of activations, AFAB keeps m
training flushes the pipeline every optimizer step; serving pipelines never drain
degrees are chosen so memory fits, communication hides and the bubble stays small

retrieve.q: Explain why TP is kept inside a node while PP is the usual cross-node axis.
answer: TP's all-reduces (or AG + RS with SP) happen inside every layer, forward and backward, and can't be hidden
PP sends one activation per stage boundary per micro-batch
measured: 1F1B drops 14% going from 1 to 2 nodes; TP ~43%

retrieve.q: Walk through 1F1B on 4 GPUs with 8 micro-batches: when GPU 3 starts its first backward, how many micro-batches GPU 0 holds at most, and where the idle time sits.
answer: micro-batch 1's forward walks through GPUs 0–3, then GPU 3 runs its backward immediately
each GPU then alternates one forward, one backward
GPU 0 holds at most p = 4 micro-batches' activations
idle time is the fill at the start and the drain at the end: 9 of 33 units (37.5% of useful time)

retrieve.q: A fixed 16.8M-token batch moves from 8,192 to 16,384 H100s. Where do you put the extra DP degree, and what does it cost?
answer: DP64 → DP128 halves the sequences per pipeline (32 → 16)
fewer micro-batches per PP16 pipeline → bigger bubble (46.9% → 93.8% of useful time at v = 1, one sequence per micro-batch, illustrative)
MFU fell 43% → 41% in Llama 3
alternatives: interleave (v > 1), or move degree into CP/PP

compare.q: Course 6 ran PP for serving with no bubble problem. What does a training step have that serving doesn't, and which schedule choice exists only because of it?
answer: a backward pass, activations held until it runs, and a synchronized optimizer step that flushes the pipeline
serving streams requests continuously, so stages never drain
1F1B, interleaving and zero-bubble schedules exist to fight the flush bubble and the held activations

compare.q: Megatron II derived TP's limit for serving; this card applies the Scaling Book's limit F > Y·C/W to training. What sets the ceiling in both, and why does it land at about 8 on H100s?
answer: TP's collectives scale with the activations while its math scales with F/Y, so beyond Y ≈ F/(C/W) comms outlast math
C/W ≈ 2,200 in a node gives ~13-way for F = 28,672, but the node has 8 GPUs, so 8 binds first
beyond the node, bandwidth drops and the Playbook measures large drops at TP16 and TP32

compare.q: Ring attention appears in course 4 for long prompts and here as CP. What is the same, and why does Llama 3's training CP all-gather K/V instead of passing it around a ring?
answer: same: split the sequence, and each GPU needs every earlier token's K and V
Llama 3 all-gathers: GQA's K/V are small, attention is O(S²) vs O(S) for the gather, and it handles document masks more easily
the ring overlaps communication with compute; the gather is simpler but on the critical path

predict.q: A pipeline has p = 8 stages and m = 16 micro-batches under 1F1B. Commit to the bubble as a share of useful time, then predict what v = 2 interleaving and doubling m to 32 each do. Which one also raises the memory held at GPU 0?
predict.answer: (p−1)/m = 7/16 = 43.75%. v = 2: 7/32 = 21.9%. m = 32: also 21.9%. Both give the same cut. Interleaving holds more activations at GPU 0 (more than p micro-batches, as in the card's 5.5 vs 4) and sends v× more point-to-point traffic; doubling m keeps 1F1B's p micro-batches of activations but needs twice as many sequences per pipeline, which a fixed global batch may not have.

apply.task: Lay out Llama 3 405B on 4,096 H100s with the same 16.8M-token batch (2,048 sequences of 8,192). Use TP8 × PP16 × DP32. (1) Check the GPU count. (2) Sequences per pipeline, and the 1F1B bubble at one sequence per micro-batch with v = 1. (3) Model state per GPU at 16 bytes per parameter with FSDP over DP32 sharding grads and optimizer only (the card's method: params 2Ψ ÷ 128, grads + optimizer 14Ψ ÷ (128 × 32)). (4) Say whether this layout is limited by memory or by something else.
apply.done: (1) 8 × 16 × 32 = 4,096. (2) 2,048 ÷ 32 = 64 sequences, bubble 15/64 = 23.4% of useful time. (3) 6.33 + 1.38 = 7.71 GB per GPU. (4) Not memory: ~72 GB is free; the bubble and compute time bind, which is why Llama 3 used more GPUs for FLOPs, not for memory.
apply.hint: The card's own 8,192-GPU row had 32 sequences per pipeline and 7.0 GB per GPU; with DP halved, each pipeline sees twice the sequences.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that interleaving and doubling m cut the bubble equally, or which one costs memory?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why 1F1B changes memory but not time?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: fixed global batch → fewer micro-batches → bigger bubble, or TP collectives → critical path → NVLink only?
Could you say from a symptom (doesn't fit, too long, comm stops hiding) which axis to add?
What will you revisit before the precision and recompute card?
